hints: Do not be distracted by the huge $1000 \text{ nm}$ size of Pandora viruses. Focus on what is true for ALL viruses, big or small: are they made of cells, and what surrounds their genome?
Remember the big difference from cells: a cell always has both DNA and RNA, but a single virus particle carries only one type of nucleic acid inside its protein capsid.
walkthrough:
**Start with what makes a virus a virus**

Think of a virus as a tiny parcel, not a cell. It has no cytoplasm, no membrane-bound organelles and no cell structure at all.

So statement 1, non-cellular, is true for all viruses, even giant Pandora viruses.

**Recall the two-part structure**

Every virus has the same basic plan: nucleic acid in the centre plus a protein coat around it, called the capsid.

So statement 2, protein coat, is also true.

**Apply the DNA or RNA rule**

Cells always contain both DNA and RNA together. Viruses are different. One virus particle contains either DNA or RNA, never both at once.

So statement 3 is false and statement 4 is true. That gives 1, 2 and 4.

options.A: Includes 3, both DNA and RNA, which is wrong. No virus contains both types of nucleic acid in the same particle.
options.B: Correctly combines 1, 2 and 4. All viruses are non-cellular, have a protein coat, and carry either DNA or RNA.
options.C: Wrong on both counts. It includes 3 which is false, and leaves out 2 and 4 which are both essential features.
options.D: 2 and 4 are true, but this misses out 1. Being non-cellular is an essential defining feature of all viruses.
